Marco David said:

We are working on an update with links, at least to the Wikipedia pages that exist for most theorems.

I've not looked at all cases, but at least for the first, "The Spectral Theorem", I don't think this is sufficient.

For example, the Spectral Theorem Wikipedia page states versions for the finite dimensional case, compact self-adjoint operators, bounded self-adjoint operators, unbounded self-adjoint operators... So simply linking to the page Spectral Theorem would even leave it unclear as to which informal statement is being considered.

I know it'd be lots of work, but Lean formalizations of the statements of the theorems would be of most use. What might help in this regard is pulling from existing efforts, e.g. the ongoing project to formalize the Spectral Theorem.

Yoh Tanimoto said:

as for the spectral theorem (for infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces), we need to define integral of vector-valued measures, which we are working on now #26160 #28499

Maybe too "in the weeds" for here, but a vector valued measure and not a projection valued measure?

The spectral theorems I'm used to either use a standard measure, e.g. direct integral formulations, or a projection valued measure but not a vector valued measure.

I assume there's some technical reason for the choice and as I'm not "in the weeds" with the code I don't see it.

"vector" in the generic sense. it is to say that it's not enough to consider docs#MeasureTheory.Measure which is ℝ≥0∞-valued. But what is needed for the spectral theory is really the Hilbert-space-valued measure (countably additive). Or projection-valued measure but in the strong operator topology (pointwise convegence topology) and not the norm topology.
There's already docs#Matrix.IsHermitian.spectral_theorem, which is the finite-dimensional Hermitian case (doesn't include infinite-dimensional, or general normal operators)

Jason Rute said:

What are the main barriers to formalizing these theorems? Are the proofs very long? Is there a lot of background needed in Mathlib to even state them?

Much like Freek Wiedijk's 100 list, the difficulty varies a lot.

Some of them (like the spectral theorem) can be stated in very physics-free language, are very much within reach, and make a lot of sense for Mathlib. Some, like Monogamy of entanglement, are essentially a pure mathematical statement but need several auxiliary definitions first (and there's quite a lot of room for what the right formal statement would be!), but then would be a pretty reasonable and short proof.

For contrast - the adiabatic theorem is pretty short to prove, but very much a "physics-y" statement. Wikipedia states it as:

A physical system remains in its instantaneous eigenstate if a given perturbation is acting on it slowly enough and if there is a gap between the eigenvalue and the rest of the Hamiltonian's spectrum.

What is "slowly enough"? And "remains in its ... eigenstate" is false for any nonzero perturbation. The correct statement is something like "in the limit of the perturbation going to infinite slowness while keeping the gap bounded away from zero, the maximum distance from remaining in an eigenstate goes to zero". And then lots of other messiness

Some theorems on the list like BQP ⊆ PP or The Threshold Theorem are not hard to state and there's really just one correct way to state them, and the proofs on paper are not hard. But the proofs in Lean would be a massive pain for the usual reasons that anything to do with computation is hard, i.e., actually spelling out every algorithm manually. MIP* = RE is also made harder by this reason, but it is not an easy proof on paper and is a very deep result. CFT central charge is its entanglement entropy would not be particularly hard to state, and the proof is not crazy on paper, but the proof (as I understand) goes through several different formulations of 'obviously equivalent' physical systems, like CFTs, explicit QFTs, VOAs... and you need to prove the correctness of each of these links, which I think might end up pulling in a lot of heavy analysis
not sure about CFT central charge is its entanglement entropy. how do you define entanglement entropy in CFT?

Yoh Tanimoto said:

not sure about CFT central charge is its entanglement entropy. how do you define entanglement entropy in CFT?

AFAIK entanglement entropy, which here means the von Neumann entropy of a reduced density matrix, is not equal to the central charge but it's proportional with a proportionally constant that goes like natural log of the system's size, e.g. [1].

PS: All of this is in a 1+1 CFT. In higher dimensions the analog is the Ryu-Takayanagi formula.
The problem is in QFT you don't have the reduced density matrix (because you don't have the trace).

Yoh Tanimoto said:

The problem is in QFT you don't have the reduced density matrix (because you don't have the trace).

I agree

PS: Though including gravity can give rise to exceptions, e.g. [1][2]
I don't think this gives entanglement entropy of CFT. Its connection to gravity seems at best speculative to me
I think that, even without a trace, you can get relative entropy rigorously in the QFT, and then use to derive an expression for entanglement entropy

Alex Meiburg said:

I think that, even without a trace, you can get relative entropy rigorously in the QFT, and then use to derive an expression for entanglement entropy

Do you mean an expression for the difference in entanglement entropy?

Yoh Tanimoto said:

I don't think this gives entanglement entropy of CFT.

AFAIK the von Neumann entropy of the reduced density matrix is the definition of entanglement entropy. As to if the definition makes sense, e.g. is finite, that's a different question.

@Alex Meiburg if you do that, for an algebra of type III, you always get infinity.

@Kelly Davis if you take the crossed product, it is no longer the original algebra of CFT.

Do you mean an expression for the difference in entanglement entropy?

Yes, but I thought I vaguely recalled there was some way to get the entanglement entropy itself from this. Like by comparing to some appropriate reference state or something. I don't know. If Yoh says this doesn't work I trust him, it's not my area of expertise. :)
it's Lemma 6.9, Theorem 6.10 of Ohya-Petz. the formula works for finite-dimensional cases.

Yoh Tanimoto said:

Kelly Davis if you take the crossed product, it is no longer the original algebra of CFT.

Yes this is true.

However, AFAIK one is forced to go to the crossed product once one takes into account the coupling of the black hole to the fields external to it.

Alternatively formulated, keeping the original algebra is equivalent to claiming the black hole does not interact with the quantum fields external to it.

My opinion is that keeping the original algebra is more problematic/unphysical than going to the crossed product.

Crossed product is just one of infinitely many ways to modify the algebra. "One is forced" seems to me speculative at best.

Anyway I don't think any of these claims related with quantum gravity is formalizable at the moment

Yoh Tanimoto said:

Crossed product is just one of infinitely many ways to modify the algebra. "One is forced" seems to me speculative at best.

The O(G) corrections in the bulk correspond to O(1/N²) corrections on the boundary. The O(1/N²) corrections on the boundary are the ones that modify the algebra to the crossed product. So in this context, "forced" doesn't seem an overreach.

That said, I agree that none of these claims related to quantum gravity seem formalizable at the moment.
Introducing N in the context of general quantum gravity coupled to QFT is already speculative to me.

We just set up PhyslibAlpha (see discussion here: #Physlib > PhyslibAlpha ). The idea being that there is a lower and quicker review standard (more applicable to AI generated content). I was thinking that within this scope, it might be worth tackling some of the items in this list.
Just sent in a PR of the Stinespring Dilation theorem (number 54 on the Top 100 Quantum list) to PhyslibAlpha.
I'd like to note that a significantly different statement of Stinespring is here. They look pretty different (in the Lean statements), I wonder if there's a way to combine them or share some code!

I think tasks of the form "Take this result in PhyslibAlpha and make it more closely tied with the results already in Physlib, with the future eye on upstreaming" is a great task for people with spare AI tokens or time who want to contribute to the project :).

Nice! Regarding the line that says Tracing out the two left parts of the output: why not just one left part?

Mine was aiming to show that you accomplish with a unitary, not just an isometry - but this requires, generally, padding the channel more. To pad A -> B to a unitary, the cleanest I could come up with was to say that AxBxB -> AxBxB traces down. AxB -> AxB isn't, in general, enough degrees of freedom I don't think.
Hmm... mine definitely has unitaries, obtained by extending an orthonormal set to an orthonormal basis (see definitions like onbPart)

Hmm. Consider the CPTP map from a 1-dimensional Hilbert space A to a 2-dimensional Hilbert space B, that gives the fully mixed state on the output space. If we wanted to enlarge this to a unitary (A * B) -> (A * B), we have a 2x2 unitary. The input state is precisely the ancillary pure state, and we apply a unitary, so we must get a pure state out, so we can't get the fully mixed state, and we can't realize this map.
Oh, maybe your ancilla state isn't pure? I'm always augmenting the input with an all-zeros state
I think you can get away with something smaller, but this notion of "purification" doesn't let you define complementary channels any more (e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0509101)
but it's obviously still useful in other contexts!
Ah I see... I made my Kraus operators all square matrices for some reason (probably because I was focused on quantum finite automata). Should be interesting to generalize.
